free_tier.stated: VPS-4, the first row of the vendor's own live VPS table: 1 vCPU, 1 GB RAM, 20 GB storage, 8 TB of traffic, USD 4 per month. The rest of the table is VPS-5 at USD 5 (1 vCPU, 2 GB, 20 GB, 8 TB), VPS-10 at USD 10 (2 vCPU, 4 GB, 40 GB, 8 TB), VPS-12T at USD 12 (1 vCPU, 1 GB, 20 GB, 24 TB), VPS-15 at USD 15 (2 vCPU, 8 GB, 80 GB, 16 TB), VPS-20 at USD 20 (4 vCPU, 8 GB, 160 GB, 16 TB), VPS-22T at USD 22 (1 vCPU, 2 GB, 20 GB, 36 TB), VPS-25 at USD 25 (4 vCPU, 16 GB, 240 GB, 16 TB), VPS-30T at USD 30 (1 vCPU, 2 GB, 20 GB, 48 TB), VPS-35 at USD 35 (8 vCPU, 16 GB, 240 GB, 24 TB) and VPS-50 at USD 50 (16 vCPU, 32 GB, 360 GB, 32 TB). The page states 19 locations and gives the filter range, but the row itself does not name a location. The tracker lists the USD 4.00 plan in Dallas, Phoenix and Toronto on a 1 Gbps port.

egress.terms: monthly traffic allowance stated per row; the page does not state whether it counts inbound, outbound or both, and publishes no overage rate

interface_detail: inferred from the tooling the provider documents; not probed
tooling: KVM with full root and a control panel; the vendor also sells bare metal and hybrid dedicated. The VPS table is rendered client-side, so a text-only fetch of the page returns placeholder rows and no prices
chaining: the VPS-12T, VPS-22T and VPS-30T rows are cheapest per terabyte: 24 TB for USD 12 and 48 TB for USD 30 with only 1 vCPU and 2 GB, which is exactly the shape of an egress relay that streams bytes and stores almost nothing

limits.value: 8 TB of traffic against 20 GB of disk and 1 GB of RAM; the VPS-12T row at USD 12 shows the same 1 vCPU and 1 GB with 24 TB, so for a pure egress node the traffic-to-price ratio triples at three times the price
